description: Passionate about space exploration, astronomy, and innovative technology. Working on Lunar Landing Site Navigator to explore and evaluate potential lunar landing sites using lunar data, terrain analysis, and visualization, helping identify suitable locations for future lunar missions. The goal is to combine technology and scientific insights to make lunar exploration more accessible and effective. 🌕🚀
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers a question every south-pole mission planner faces: will this site, on this date, actually have sunlight and Earth contact — once real terrain gets in the way? Most tools stop at geometric sun/Earth angles. We go further: using NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL SPICE ephemeris, we compute the actual local horizon at each site and determine when the Sun or Earth clears real crater rims and ridges, not just an idealized flat horizon.

The centerpiece is a Mission Delay Simulator — move a landing date and instantly see how sunlight, communication windows, and solar power change, which directly addresses NASA’s call to handle schedule slips and hardware delays. We validated this against real landing sites (IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3), with every result traceable to its data source, resolution, and assumptions — and sites with insufficient terrain data are labeled honestly rather than given a fabricated number.

It matters because mission planning decisions shouldn’t rest on optimistic geometry when the Moon’s terrain says otherwise.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers two questions that decide a south-pole landing: when does sunlight reach the lander, and when is Earth in view for a direct link? It then shows how far each answer can be trusted.

How it works. Pick a site and dates. The Python engine computes the Sun and Earth directions from NASA/JPL SPICE (DE440). It builds the terrain horizon at every compass direction from real LRO LOLA elevation data (20 m at IM-2), by tracing rays over the Moon's curved surface. It then finds when each body is visible, to 1-second resolution, as intervals, fractions of time, the longest dark stretch, and a countdown to sunset and Earthset. Everything is recomputed at 8 displaced positions (default ±100 m), so every number comes with a band. The browser only displays what the engine computed.

What you get. Terrain-corrected and geometric (no terrain) results are shown side by side. For IM-2 Athena (15 Jan 2027, 30 days) the Sun is visible 48.6 % of the time (band 45.4–48.9 %) against 53.3 % geometric, and Earth 80.8 % against 73.5 %. A delay simulator shows how a schedule slip moves the window, and a comparison view puts sites and dates side by side. A time player, click-to-pick map on NASA imagery, Learn mode and glossary make it usable by non-specialists.

Intended impact. Mission planners, educators and the public can compare sites and dates in seconds, instead of working through several specialist tools for each combination.

What makes it creative. The design is honesty-first. Where terrain data is insufficient (IM-1), the tool says "terrain data insufficient" and gives no number. Every result states its status: "validated" means reviewed and approved by the project owner, not proven against measurement, and the Chandrayaan-3 terrain is labelled "implemented unvalidated". It is geometry only: no link budget, thermal or power model.

Tools. Python 3.12, FastAPI, SpiceyPy/NAIF SPICE, rasterio/GDAL, NumPy; React, TypeScript, Vite; pytest, Vitest, axe-core and a real-browser end-to-end suite (404 backend, 188 frontend and 26 browser checks pass); Docker. Data: NASA LOLA elevation models (PGDA), NAIF kernels, LROC imagery via NASA Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons as an implementation check. It runs on an ordinary laptop with no special hardware.

What we considered. Scientific accuracy over visuals: no invented data, typed errors, and checksum-verified data. The ephemeris matches JPL Horizons to 1.4×10⁻⁸° and the horizon matches an independent implementation to 1.1×10⁻⁹°. We documented 39 limitations and made setup reproducible with a verified data bundle and Docker.

Code and docs: github.com/Dhinu-2001/NASA-Space-Apps-2026 (MIT licence). Independent project, not endorsed by NASA.
